coredata.dc:description: Heterojunction photocatalysts have dominated the area of photocatalysis owing to their synergistic interactions among the integrated components, which not only enhance charge carrier separation but also prompt full-scale solar energy utilization. Construction of carbon nitride(CN) and bismuth sulfide(BS) heterojunctions has also been considered as an effective strategy to promote the spatial separation of photogenerated electron-hole pairs and achieve enhanced photocatalytic activity. In this paper, heterojunction photocatalysts composed of Bi₂S₃ and non-metallic element-doped g-C₃N₄ (xCN-BS, where x stands for O, S, or P) were prepared using a hydrothermal method. Among these photocatalysts, oxygen-doped OCN-BS demonstrated excellent photocatalytic degradation of pollutants. When a BPA solution with a concentration of 15 mg/L was treated with OCN-BS, the removal rate of BPA could reach 96 % within 4 h. The photocatalytic degradation of pollutants was carried out using OCN-BS. Meanwhile, after 5 cycle experiments, the photocatalytic activity of OCN-BS could still be maintained at 88 %, demonstrating good stability. In addition, the formation of the heterojunction narrowed the band gap width of the composites, and the xCN-BS composites exhibited more intense light absorption in the wavelength range of 200–1200 nm, with the light absorption threshold disappearing, indicating a wider light absorption range. The construction of the BS and xCN heterojunction further enhanced the photocatalytic degradation of pollutants while avoiding the dissolution of bismuth metal, thereby addressing the issue of poor material stability and achieving the effect of “killing two birds with one stone.” Therefore, the effective separation of photogenerated charge pairs through the construction of heterojunctions provides potential insights for the improvement of photocatalytic degradation of BPA in water.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Heterojunction photocatalysts have dominated the area of photocatalysis owing to their synergistic interactions among the integrated components, which not only enhance charge carrier separation but also prompt full-scale solar energy utilization. Construction of carbon nitride(CN) and bismuth sulfide(BS) heterojunctions has also been considered as an effective strategy to promote the spatial separation of photogenerated electron-hole pairs and achieve enhanced photocatalytic activity. In this paper, heterojunction photocatalysts composed of Bi₂S₃ and non-metallic element-doped g-C₃N₄ (xCN-BS, where x stands for O, S, or P) were prepared using a hydrothermal method. Among these photocatalysts, oxygen-doped OCN-BS demonstrated excellent photocatalytic degradation of pollutants. When a BPA solution with a concentration of 15 mg/L was treated with OCN-BS, the removal rate of BPA could reach 96 % within 4 h. The photocatalytic degradation of pollutants was carried out using OCN-BS. Meanwhile, after 5 cycle experiments, the photocatalytic activity of OCN-BS could still be maintained at 88 %, demonstrating good stability. In addition, the formation of the heterojunction narrowed the band gap width of the composites, and the xCN-BS composites exhibited more intense light absorption in the wavelength range of 200–1200 nm, with the light absorption threshold disappearing, indicating a wider light absorption range. The construction of the BS and xCN heterojunction further enhanced the photocatalytic degradation of pollutants while avoiding the dissolution of bismuth metal, thereby addressing the issue of poor material stability and achieving the effect of “killing two birds with one stone.” Therefore, the effective separation of photogenerated charge pairs through the construction of heterojunctions provides potential insights for the improvement of photocatalytic degradation of BPA in water.

ce:section.ce:para: Environmental pollution is an unavoidable problem in today's society. Bisphenol A (BPA) is widely used industrially to synthesize materials such as polycarbonate (PC) and epoxy resins. However, BPA poses a significant threat to health and the environment due to its endocrine-disrupting properties [1,2]. It is well known that the solubility of BPA in aqueous environments ranges from 120 to 300 mg/L [3]. Consequently, BPA is present in various water sources, including drinking water, surface water, and industrial wastewater. Meanwhile, numerous strategies for BPA degradation have emerged, including biodegradation, advanced oxidation processes (AOP) (such as photocatalysis or ozonation) [4], and BPA adsorption[5]. Photocatalytic technology is characterized by low cost, high pollutant degradation efficiency, green, non-toxic and no secondary pollution, which is a feasible way to solve the problem effectively [6].

Graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4, CN) is composed of the earth's abundant non-metallic elements carbon and nitrogen. It is obtained by the direct condensation of nitrogen-rich organic precursors, such as urea and melamine, through a thermal polymerization process [7,8]. CN exhibits good visible light activity and demonstrates excellent catalytic performance in the field of pollutant degradation. This is attributed to its unique off-domain conjugated structure, which facilitates effective charge separation and transfer [9]. Additionally, CN offers a cost-effective, non-toxic, environmentally friendly synthesis process and biocompatibility. Depending on the requirements, the properties of CN can be modulated through methods such as elemental doping, construction of heterojunctions, noble metal deposition, and defect engineering[10]. These modifications improve light absorption and enhance the separation efficiency of electron-hole pairs, thereby further enhancing the photocatalytic activity. Currently, modifications by a single method may no longer suffice to meet the demands for performance enhancement. Therefore, combining multiple modification methods is an effective strategy.

Bismuth sulfide (Bi2S3, BS) is a semiconductor material widely used in photocatalysis, known for its advantageous properties such as good light absorption, low preparation cost, and a narrow bandgap. However, BS faces some limitations in its applications, most notably the rapid recombination of electron-hole pairs and photo-corrosion of the material under light exposure. When BS forms a heterojunction with elementally doped CN, a built-in electric field is created due to the differences in the properties of the two materials. This built-in electric field can effectively separate photogenerated electrons and holes, enhancing the stability of the catalyst and achieving a dual benefit.

In the heterojunction of BS and CN, photogenerated electrons tend to migrate into CN. This migration reduces the electron concentration on the surface of BS [11]. Consequently, the likelihood of photogenerated electrons reacting with oxygen on the BS surface is diminished, thereby decreasing the risk of surface oxidation. The high chemical stability and corrosion resistance of CN were recognized [12]. Particularly in photocatalytic applications, CN can withstand the effects of photo-corrosion and chemical corrosion to a significant extent.

Analyzing the xCN-BS heterojunction material from the economic point of view. Firstly, the raw materials for preparing BS and CN are inexpensive and widely available, which makes the cost of preparing xCN-BS heterojunctions lower. Secondly, the preparation of xCN-BS heterojunction materials is done using the hydrothermal method. This method has the advantages of low energy consumption and environmental friendliness. And it can be prepared on a large scale, which has the potential for commercialization. Finally, the formation of xCN-BS heterojunctions greatly improves the stability of the material, thereby enabling better application in the water treatment process.

In this paper, a series of modifications were conducted on carbon nitride, based on the strategy of combined elemental doping and heterojunction construction, to identify the most suitable modification scheme. The effects of doping different non-metallic elements (O, S, and P) on the properties of carbon nitride were longitudinally explored, with each element being doped separately. Horizontally, the impact of different doping ratios on the properties of carbon nitride was examined, and four distinct ratios were tested. Finally, the influence of heterojunction construction on the electron transfer characteristics of carbon nitride materials was analyzed. Provide valuable ideas for exploring the progress of heterojunction materials to facilitate the directional transfer of photogenerated electrons.

Oxygen-doped carbon nitride was synthesized through the thermal polymerization of 40 g of urea with varying masses of oxalic acid. The resulting material was labeled as x% OCN, where x denotes the mass percentage of oxalic acid relative to urea (x = 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10). Using a similar approach, sulfur-doped carbon nitride and phosphorus-doped carbon nitride were synthesized by replacing oxalic acid with thiourea and hexachlorotrisphosphonitrile, respectively. Subsequently, heterojunctions of bismuth sulfide with these non-metallic element-doped carbon nitrides were prepared via a hydrothermal reaction

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Quanta-TM55) was used to investigate the microstructure and morphology of the different photocatalysts. X-ray powder diffractometer (XRD, Bruker D8 Advance, Cu- Kα radiation) was used to study phase, structure, composition, and physical properties of the materials. In order to analyze the chemical valence of the catalyst surface X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo ESCALAB 250Xi) was adopted. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy was performed within 500–4000 cm−1 (FT-IR, Nexus 870 model). Photoluminescence (PL) spectra were obtained by fluorescence spectrophotometer (Hitachi, F-4500) using 470 nm as the excitation source. Using a PerkinElmer Lambda 750S UV-Vis spectrometer with a wavelength range of 300–800 nm. The photoluminescence spectra of the catalysts were tested using an FL3-TCSPC fluorescence spectrometer. The photocurrent test, electrochemical impedance spectra, and Mott Schottky test were carried out using a CHI660B electrochemical workstation manufactured by Shanghai Chenhua Instrument Company.

In the photocatalytic experiments, 30 mg of catalyst and 50 mL of a BPA solution at a concentration of 15 mg/L were homogeneously mixed in a quartz-tube reactor. The mixture was then subjected to 2 min of sonication to ensure a uniform dispersion of the catalyst. Following this, the mixture was continuously stirred in the dark for 1 h to establish the adsorption-desorption equilibrium between the catalyst and the solution. Subsequently, a light source (a 300 W xenon lamp) was turned on, and 1 mL of the sample was collected at specific time intervals. The photocatalyst and solution were separated using a 0.22 µm filter, after which the concentration of BPA was measured using high-performance liquid chromatography (e2685, Waters) equipped with a UV–visible detector (2489, Waters). To investigate the effect of different active species on the degradation process of BPA, capture experiments were conducted using different capture agents. Sodium oxalate (Na2C2O4), tert-butanol (t-ButOH), and 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidinium-nitrogen-oxide (TEMPOL) were used as trapping agents for photogenerated holes (h+), hydroxyl radicals (·OH), and superoxide radicals (-O2 -), respectively.

The stability of the activity of the catalyst was evaluated using a recycling experiment. Then after each experiment, the remaining solution with catalyst suspended was collected for filtration, washing, drying and then used in the next round of experiments. Multiple cycles of experiments were conducted to evaluate the catalysts’ stability.

From the SEM images of the prepared CN-BS depicted in Fig. 1a, it was found that the CN exhibited a uniformly distributed block structure measuring approximately 2 μm in size. BS particles were observed to be distributed on the surface of the CN block structures, resulting in a complex and ordered interfacial structure. The formation of the block structure was considered important for the photocatalytic effect, as it was capable of providing a large number of reaction sites. Concurrently, it facilitated the separation of photogenerated electrons and holes through the heterojunction interface, thereby enhancing the photocatalytic activity. The OCN-BS photocatalyst, as shown in Fig. 1b, was noted to exhibit a rod-like microstructure. This distinct shape of OCN-BS may have had a significant impact on the catalytic performance, as differences in morphology typically lead to alterations in the distribution of active sites. From the particle size distribution graph (Fig. S2), it is found that the average particle size of the prepared nanocomposites is 435.4 ± 0.404 nm[13]. The catalyst particles were found to exhibit a blocky structure, which can be attributed to the stacking properties of the carbon nitride material, as revealed by the analysis of the particle size distribution map in conjunction with the SEM spectra.

The emergence of the rod-like structure was attributed to a rolling mechanism [14]. According to this mechanism, the layer structure was observed to curl after the interlayer forces of the CN lamellar structure had been disrupted. Subsequently, the CN, with the curled layer serving as a growth precursor, gradually developed into a nanorod-like structure. The growth mechanism could be delineated in the following manner: Initially, the ultrasonic process was found to strip the CN bulk structure, yielding a small number of nanosheets. Subsequently, the hydrothermal reaction process further stripped the CN bulk structure, while the stripped lamellar structure began to curl from the edges as the temperature and pressure rose. Ultimately, under specific conditions, the CN was observed to grow progressively into a nanorod-like structure based on the curled lamellar structure [15].

Further observation of Fig. 1c and Fig. 1d revealed that the SCN-BS and PCN-BS catalysts possessed larger bulk structures, measuring approximately 3.5 μm in size. BS particles were noted to be distributed on the surfaces of these catalysts. However, a reduced number of CN rod structures were observed, which was attributed to the concentration of ions in the system and the anisotropy of the crystal structure. It was noted that higher temperatures favored the anisotropic growth of the crystal structure. It was speculated that SCN and PCN underwent thermal decomposition during the synthesis of the heterojunction at elevated temperatures. The synthesis process was conducted in an aerobic environment, which was believed to have caused the doped S and P elements to be oxidized, transforming them into acid radicals. The resulting acid radical anions were suspected to have influenced the layer structure in a metastable state, inducing its collapse. This was considered to have resulted in a reduction of the key precursors necessary for the growth of the rod structure, and as a consequence, no CN rod structure was generated [16].

The crystal structure of the catalyst samples was analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD). The XRD patterns of BS, CN-BS, OCN-BS, SCN-BS and PCN-BS are shown in Fig. 2a. The XRD diffractograms were compared with the standard card of orthorhombic phase Bi2S3 (PDF No. 17–0320) [17,18]. The diffraction peaks at 22.4°, 24.9°,25.2°,27.4°,28.6°, 31.8°, and 46.5° correspond to (220), (130), (310), (021), (211), (221), and (431), and the crystal structure belongs to the orthorhombic system, which is consistent with the data in the standard card (PDF No. 17–0320). From the XRD patterns, a new characteristic diffraction peak appeared at 27.2°, corresponding to the (002) crystal plane of CN, which can be attributed to the interlayer stacking structure of conjugated aromatic systems[19]. These changes imply the formation of a heterojunction interface between BS and CN.

The analysis of the XRD spectra of OCN-BS, SCN-BS, and PCN-BS shows a relatively obvious difference in the characteristic peaks at the 27.2° (002) crystal plane. These changes in the characteristic peaks can be attributed to the doping of nonmetallic elements, which distorts the structure of CN while decreasing the interlayer spacing of CN, thus increasing the density of CN. The diffraction peaks become sharp due to the increase in the degree of CN condensation[20,21]. Meanwhile, the peak at (002) belongs to the interlayer stacking, and the decrease of the peak indicates that the amount of interlayer stacking is small, and the lumpy shape turns into a layer. This can also be corroborated laterally by the appearance of more lumpy CN in OCN-BS, corresponding to the appearance of rod-like CN in the SEM spectra. A cluster of characteristic peaks was observed in the range of 27.2–28.7°. The characteristic diffraction peak on the left was attributed to the (002) crystal plane of CN, and the characteristic diffraction peak on the right was attributed to the (021) crystal plane of BS. The characteristic peak around 38° was attributed to the BS (024) crystal plane[22].

The surface functional groups of BS, CN-BS, OCN-BS, SCN-BS and PCN-BS samples were analyzed using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), and the results are shown in Fig. 2b. For the CN-BS sample, a broad peak near 3100 cm−1 can be observed, the formation of which originates from H2O molecules adsorbed on the surface of the sample and the uncondensed amine groups (N-H vibration) [23]. In addition, the presence of characteristic peaks at 1400 cm−1, 1312 cm−1 and 1232 cm−1 is attributed to the typical stretching vibrational mode of the heptazine heterocycle (C6N7)[24,25]. A characteristic peak at 890 cm−1 was also observed, corresponding to the deformation vibration of N-H. A strong and sharp characteristic peak at 780 cm−1, which was attributed to the characteristic breathing mode of the triazine unit, corresponded to the condensed CN heterocycle [26]. A weak peak at 1726 cm−1 attributed to the vibrational peak of -COOH. The FT-IR of the OCN-BS, SCN-BS and PCN-BS samples did not show significant new peaks as compared to CN-BS, indicating that the doping of other non-metallic elements did not result in the appearance of new functional groups.

The electron arrangement and chemical bonding of the elements in the catalyst were observed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The C 1 s spectra of CN-BS are displayed in Fig. 3a, with characteristic peaks corresponding to C-C and sp2-C at 284.8 eV and 288.1 eV, respectively[27]. A new characteristic peak at 289.6 eV, corresponding to -COOH, was observed in OCN-BS. Similarly, characteristic peaks were observed in SCN-BS and PCN-BS at 288.9 eV[28]. At the same time, it was found that the -COOH surface functional group appeared in all three materials, which is favorable for the nucleation growth of bismuth sulfide. The appearance of -COOH surface functional groups was also attributed to the carbon nitride pyrolysis.

The N 1 s spectrum of CN-BS, as shown in Fig. 3b, exhibits three characteristic peaks at 398.5 eV, 399.7 eV, and 401.1 eV, corresponding to CN-C, N-C3, and C-N-H, respectively[29]. The positions of these characteristic peaks had been shifted. This shift was mainly attributed to the doping of different nonmetallic elements. Since different nonmetallic elements possess varying electronegativities, the introduction of these elements into the materials and their formation of chemical bonds could lead to a redistribution of the electron density. This redistribution was considered to be the cause of the position shift of the N 1 s peak [30].

The Bi 4 f and S 2p spectra (Fig. 3c) reveal information about the valence states of Bi and S. In the Bi 4 f spectrum of CN-BS, the peaks at 157.9 eV and 163.2 eV are attributed to Bi 4 f7/2 and Bi 4 f5/2 of Bi3+, respectively. The S 2p spectra display peaks at binding energies of 158.8 eV and 160.5 eV, which are assigned to S 2p3/2 and S 2p1/2, confirming that the predominant valence state of sulfur is S2-. The XPS analysis of the Bi 4 f and S 2p spectra indicates that the valence states of Bi and S in the heterojunction are consistent with those in Bi2S3, suggesting that the elemental valence state of Bi in the heterojunction structure is stable and does not undergo oxidation[31].

From Fig. 3c, it was clearly observable that OCN-BS exhibited a significant shift compared to other materials. This shift was primarily attributed to the difference in electronegativity; oxygen, having a high electronegativity, altered the electron cloud density during the formation of heterojunctions, resulting in a reduced electron cloud density for BS and consequently an increased binding energy. Furthermore, the shift was attributed to the doping distortion, which caused a distortion in the CN crystal structure due to the introduction of non-metallic elements. This distortion also occurred during the formation of heterojunctions, leading to chemical shifts. The O 1 s spectrum of OCN-BS, as depicted in Fig. 3d, showed a characteristic peak at a binding energy of 531.8 eV, which was related to the chemisorption of molecular oxygen. Another peak, located at 539.7 eV, was attributed to the σ* state of the C-O bond [32,33]. No characteristic peak corresponding to Bi-O was observed in OCN-BS.

In order to fully evaluate the performance of photocatalyst, the electron transfer rate and the separation efficiency of electron-hole pairs need to be evaluated. Solid-state ultraviolet-visible diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (UV–vis DRS), photocurrent response (i-t), electrochemical impedance testing (EIS), and linear scanning voltammetry (LSV) were chosen to test the separation efficiency of photogenerated electron-hole pairs and the electron transport properties of photocatalytic materials.

As depicted in Fig. 4a, the photocurrent response of the CN-BS sample was found to be significantly superior to that of the BS sample, indicating that the formation of the heterojunction structure played an active role in enhancing the effective separation of photogenerated electrons and holes[34,35]. In addition, the photocurrent response intensities of OCN-BS, SCN-BS, and PCN-BS samples were higher than those of undoped CN-BS samples, indicating that the doping of non-metallic elements significantly promotes the separation efficiency of electrons and holes in heterojunctions. Among these modified samples, OCN-BS exhibits the highest photocurrent response, showing a result that not only demonstrates the importance of the heterojunction structure, but also emphasizes the improved effect of non-metallic element doping on the separation efficiency of photogenerated carriers.

Information on the electron transport and interfacial properties of photocatalytic materials is provided by the results of EIS. The performance of photocatalytic materials can be evaluated using frequency-domain data, which is obtained by measuring the material's response to an AC voltage. As depicted in Fig. 4b, the EIS arc radius of CN-BS was found to be significantly smaller than that of BS, suggesting that the heterojunction structure provided superior interfacial charge transfer performance[36,37]. The EIS arc radii of OCN-BS, SCN-BS, and PCN-BS were observed to be smaller than those of CN-BS, indicating that doping with nonmetallic elements enhanced the separation and migration of electron-hole pairs, thereby improving the photocatalytic performance. The transfer resistances of CN-BS and OCN-BS were determined to be 4430 Ω and 498 Ω, respectively, through testing and analysis. The transfer resistance of CN-BS was approximately 9 times higher than that of OCN-BS. The doping with non-metallic oxygen was found to reduce the transfer resistance of the material. Consequently, OCN-BS exhibited a higher charge-transfer efficiency and better electron-hole separation, leading to superior photocatalytic performance.

The LSV curves presented in Fig. 4c show the variation of current density with potential for BS, CN-BS, OCN-BS, SCN-BS and PCN-BS. By comparing these curves, the performance differences between different catalysts can be observed. The CN-BS heterojunction shows a higher photocurrent density than BS at the same voltage, which indicates a significant improvement in the internal electron-hole separation efficiency of this heterojunction[38,39]. And the OCN-BS, SCN-BS and PCN-BS materials modified with nonmetallic elements exhibit higher photocurrent densities at the same potential, which further highlights the positive effect of the elemental modification in enhancing the electron-hole separation efficiency. The photoelectric conversion efficiency of each catalyst was calculated by analyzing the LSV curves (Fig. 4d). The photoelectric conversion efficiency of BS was 0.003 %, while that of CN-BS was slightly higher at 0.007 %. However, the modified heterojunction catalysts OCN-BS, SCN-BS, and PCN-BS showed superior performance with photoelectric conversion efficiencies of 0.055 %, 0.012 %, and 0.019 %, respectively. These results indicate that the nonmetallic element modification has a significant positive effect on enhancing the photoelectric conversion efficiency of CN-BS catalysts.

UV–vis DRS of photocatalysts was commonly used to measure the light absorption capacity and to determine the light absorption range of the catalysts. As shown in Fig. 5a, CN-BS exhibited a clear absorption margin, and its light absorption ability was observed to decrease significantly when the wavelength exceeded 450 nm. Upon doping with nonmetallic elements OCN-BS, SCN-BS, and PCN-BS exhibited more intense light absorption properties within the wavelength range of 200–1000 nm, and their light absorption threshold disappeared, indicating a wider light absorption range. This suggested that doping with non-metallic elements could improve the light absorption properties of heterojunction structures, thereby enabling the catalysts to efficiently absorb photons from lower energies.

By analyzing the absorption margins and combining them with the Kubelka-Munk formula, the forbidden bandwidth of the material can be determined[40]. The bandgap energy can affect the light absorption properties of the material and also the electron transport properties.

As depicted in Fig. 5b, the bandgap energies of CN-BS, OCN-BS, SCN-BS, and PCN-BS were measured to be 2.52 eV, 2.19 eV, 2.38 eV, and 2.22 eV, respectively. The bandgap width of a material determines its ability to absorb light at different wavelengths. Catalysts with smaller bandgaps are typically more sensitive to light in the visible region, as they are capable of absorbing lower energy photons. Conversely, catalysts with larger bandgaps are more sensitive to the UV region. It was observed that the bandgap width of the catalyst could be adjusted and its absorption range extended by doping with non-metallic elements. The variation in bandgap energy indicated that doping with non-metallic elements reduced the bandgap capacity of the CN-BS heterojunction, thereby enhancing the photocatalytic performance of the material. The reduction in the heterojunction bandgap was primarily attributed to the twisting changes in the crystal structure caused by non-metallic doping and the level of doping[41].

Typically, the built-in electric field was related to the Fermi energy level of the material[42]. Energy band analysis revealed that there was a certain difference between the Fermi energy levels of BS and xCN when they were in contact, resulting in the transfer of electrons from BS to xCN. This transfer continued until the Fermi energy levels of the two materials equalized, and a space charge region formed in the contact region between BS and xCN during the electron transfer process to generate the built-in electric field. The generation of the built-in electric field led to an improvement in the separation efficiency of electron-hole pairs and also reduced the photocorrosion of BS.

Meanwhile, the non-metallic doping induces a mid-bandgap state, which also leads to the narrowing of the heterojunction bandgap[43]. The empty mid-bandgap state can accommodate electrons excited by light from the valence band of the nonmetal-doped CN-BS heterojunction. O doping produces a new hybridization energy level in the O 2p orbital[44]; P doping produces a new hybridization energy level in the P 3p orbital; and S doping produces a new hybridization energy level in the S 2p orbital[45]. This contributes to the improvement of the photocatalytic performance of the material.

The relative rates of charge separation in CN-BS, OCN-BS, SCN-BS, and PCN-BS composites were measured using PL spectroscopy at an excitation wavelength of 365 nm. As can be observed in Fig. S3, a strong peak of high intensity was observed at 436 nm for CN-BS, which was attributed to the lone pair of electrons in CN-BS that absorbed energy from the non-bonding orbitals and subsequently jumped to the anti-bonding orbitals [46]. In contrast, the PL intensities of OCN-BS, SCN-BS, and PCN-BS were observed to have decreased sharply, with the most significant decrease noted in OCN-BS. The pronounced decrease in the PL intensity of OCN-BS indicated that electrons had migrated from BS to OCN, facilitating the effective separation of charges and reducing the rate of electron-hole recombination[47]. Consequently, OCN-BS, SCN-BS, and PCN-BS exhibited enhanced catalytic activity. When the XPS data analysis was taken into account, it was found that doping with non-metal elements altered the electron cloud density. This change in electron cloud density made it more favorable for photogenerated electrons to be transferred from BS to OCN. Such electron transfer rendered the electron holes less likely to recombine, thereby reducing the electron-hole recombination rate.

In order to evaluate the performance of the photocatalysts, the photocatalytic activity was evaluated using the method of degrading BPA in water. In Fig. 6a, the photocatalytic degradation of BPA by OCN-BS with varying amounts of oxygen doping was demonstrated. To ensure that the catalyst had sufficient contact with BPA, dark reaction adsorption was carried out for 1 h prior to the experimental reaction to ensure that the photocatalyst fully adsorbed the BPA molecule (The dark reaction adsorption data are detailed in Fig. S4). In the subsequent degradation experiments, it was observed that the OCN-BS catalysts with different O doping amounts showed a certain pattern of degradation effect on BPA. Specifically, with the gradual increase of O doping, the degradation efficiency of BPA first increased and then decreased. Among this range of O doping, 5 % OCN-BS exhibited the best photocatalytic degradation performance. The experimental results indicate that the appropriate amount of O doping can effectively improve the photocatalytic activity of OCN-BS, while excessive O doping may not be conducive to the photocatalytic degradation of BPA.

In Fig. 6b, the photocatalytic degradation of BPA by sulfur-doped carbon nitride bismuth sulfide heterojunction (SCN-BS) with varying amounts of sulfur doping was demonstrated. The results indicated that the degradation efficiencies of SCN-BS catalysts with different sulfur doping levels exhibited a gradual increasing trend. It was determined that the optimal amount of sulfur doping was 10 % of SCN-BS, suggesting that an appropriate amount of sulfur element doping could effectively enhance the photocatalytic performance of SCN-BS catalysts. In Fig. 6c, the photocatalytic degradation of BPA by phosphorus-doped carbon nitride bismuth sulfide heterojunction (PCN-BS) with varying amounts of phosphorus doping was shown, where the optimal phosphorus doping was found to be 5 % PCN-BS. Similar to OCN-BS and SCN-BS, it was observed that phosphorus, as a nonmetallic element, could also improve the photocatalytic activity of heterojunction photocatalysis. The optimal degradation rates for the four materials were illustrated in Fig. 6d. It was found that the degradation rate of OCN-BS for BPA reached as high as 96 %, while the degradation rates of SCN-BS and PCN-BS were 87 % and 77 %, respectively.

To verify the importance of the heterojunction, the optimal doping amounts of three nonmetallic elements O, S, and P, in the doped heterojunction photocatalysts were selected as representative catalysts for the doping of each element. Concurrently, BS and CN were combined in a reactor and subjected to a hydrothermal treatment at 160°C for 24 h to prepare BS+CN photocatalysts. The obtained catalysts were then subjected to photocatalytic experiments. As depicted in Fig. 7a, it was found that the degradation of BPA by BS was almost negligible, whereas the degradation of BPA by CN was approximately 22 %. However, the degradation of BPA by CN-BS was enhanced to 66 %. The photocatalytic degradation of BS+CN was comparable to that of CN, indicating that the photocatalytic performance of BS+CN, which did not form a heterojunction structure, was inferior. This finding clarified the pivotal role of the heterojunction in enhancing the photocatalytic activity.

Compared with the CN-BS heterojunction, the degradation of BPA by OCN-BS, SCN-BS and PCN-BS was significantly improved, which indicated that the photocatalytic performance of the catalyst is improved by the doping of non-metallic elements. By fitting the kinetics of photocatalytic degradation of BPA, it was found to be consistent with quasi-primary kinetics. As shown in Fig. 7b, the catalytic rate of BS was only 0.01183 h−1, while the catalytic rate of CN-BS with constructed heterojunction was increased to 0.2599 h−1. The catalytic rate of the heterojunction modified with nonmetallic elements was enhanced again, with OCN-BS having the highest catalytic rate of 0.6293 h−1, which was 53.2 times higher than that of BS. These results show that the construction of heterojunction and doping of non-metallic elements can effectively enhance the photocatalyst activity.

In order to investigate the photocatalytic reaction mechanism, 5 % OCN-BS was used as a photocatalyst to probe the effect of different traps on the degradation process of BPA. Sodium oxalate (Na2C2O4), tert-butanol (t-ButOH), 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidinium-nitrogen-oxide (TEMPOL) and Furfuryl alcohol (FAA) were used as trappers to capture photogenerated holes (h+), hydroxyl radicals (·OH), superoxide radicals (·O2 -), and Singlet oxygen (1O2) respectively. When TEMPOL, t-ButOH, Na2C2O4 and FAA were added to the photocatalytic system, the degradation rate decreased from 96.2 % to 24.1 %, 73.1 % 89.7 % and 92.2 %, respectively (Fig. S5), which indicated that the main active species was ·O2 -. The degradation process is shown in the following equation[48,49]:
(2) 5%OCN-BS + simulated solar light → h+ + e-
(3) O2 + e- →·O2 -
(4) O2 - + BPA → Degradation products
(5) 2·O2 - + 2H+ →·OH
(6) ·OH + BPA → Degradation products

In order to deeply analyze the electronic energy band in the heterojunction structure, the forbidden bandwidths of the materials were determined by applying the Kubelka-Munk formula to convert the UV–vis test data. The test data are shown in Fig. S6a and Fig. S6c, with bandgap widths of 1.21 eV for BS and 2.03 eV for OCN, respectively. Further the valence band positions (EVB, XPS) of BS and OCN were measured by VBXPS test technique, and from Fig. S6b and Fig. S6d it can be seen that the EVB, XPS of BS and OCN are 1.07 eV and 1.97 eV, respectively. Converting the measured EVB, XPS gives EVB, NHE of 0.77 eV and 1.67 eV for BS and OCN, respectively. Using the formula EVB = ECB + Eg, the conduction band positions of BS and OCN were determined to be −0.44 eV and −0.36 eV. The Mott-Schottky analysis was performed on BS and OCN simultaneously (Fig. S7). The flat band potentials of BS and OCN were determined to be −0.63 eV (vs. SCE) and −0.53 eV (vs. SCE), respectively, through the analysis of their Mott-Schottky data. When converted to the standard hydrogen electrode scale, the flat band potentials of BS and OCN were found to be −0.44 eV and −0.36 eV (vs. NHE), respectively. These results are in agreement with those calculated using the formula EVB = ECB + Eg. Combined with the above analysis, the band structure of the catalyst was plotted ( Fig. 8). From the figure, it can be seen that the electron of BS jumps to the conduction band (CB) position under light excitation. OCN has a lower CB site, which facilitates electron transport from the BS to the CB of the OCN. At the CB position of OCN, the electrons react with oxygen in contact to form ·O2 -, which can participate in redox reactions during the photocatalytic process, thus promoting the degradation of organic matter.

In addition to this, the intermediate degradation products of BPA were tracked using LC-MS analysis. Based on this analysis, the possible degradation route of BPA was hypothesized (Fig. S8 and S9). Specifically, monohydroxylated BPA and dihydroxylated BPA were formed from BPA due to the addition of electrophilic groups. These compounds then underwent further dehydrogenation to form quinones. Subsequently, with the cleavage of the benzene ring, aliphatic compounds containing carboxyl groups were produced. Finally, further oxidation led to the formation of more ring-opening substances, which were eventually mineralized to carbon dioxide and water.

As shown in the previous results, the electrons in the bismuth phosphorus sulfide photocatalyst were excited and migrated to the conduction band, and during this migration, the sulfur vacancies acted as "electron traps" and some of the electrons were captured. These trapped electrons then react with oxygen, leading to the production of ·O2 -. The corrosion that occurred during this process was concentrated around the sulfur vacancies of the bismuth sulfide, which ultimately led to the damage of the catalyst. In contrast, in CN-BS photocatalysts, the electrons that were excited in the BS were transported into the CN, and the process of electron transport actually decelerated the rate at which the BS underwent photo-corrosion. In this way, the heterojunction design effectively circumvented the corrosion phenomenon of BS and enhanced the stability of the catalyst.

In order to explore the effects of catalyst dosage, initial concentration of pollutants and pH value of solution on photocatalytic degradation, a series of conditioned experiments were conducted using 5 % OCN-BS photocatalyst with the best degradation effect. Fig. 9a and Fig. 9b show the degradation effect of BPA under different 5 % OCN-BS catalyst dosing. It can be found that with the increase of catalyst dosage, the degradation efficiency of BPA shows a trend of first increasing and then saturation. An increase in catalyst dosage provides more active sites for the reaction and accelerates the reaction rate[50,51]. However, excessive catalyst dosage does not significantly improve the reaction effect, due to the possibility of shielding the light source from irradiation by excessive catalyst dosage[52]. At the same time, a larger number of catalysts has the potential to undergo particle agglomeration, affecting the homogeneous structure of the suspension and reducing the number of active sites.

Fig. 9c demonstrates the photocatalytic degradation of 5 % OCN-BS at different initial concentrations of BPA, and the photocatalytic degradation efficiency gradually increases as the initial concentration of BPA decreases in the reaction. The degradation of 5 mg/L of BPA was completed in 3 h when the catalyst was injected at a concentration of 0.6 g/L. However, when the BPA concentration was increased to 10 mg/L or 15 mg/L, it took 4 h for BPA to complete degradation. When the concentration of BPA increased to 20 mg/L or 30 mg/L, the photocatalytic degradation rate of the catalyst began to decrease significantly, which may be caused by insufficient active sites. Higher concentrations of BPA are detrimental to the photocatalytic degradation process, which may be due to the fact that higher concentrations of the pollutant occupy the initial reactive sites, thus delaying the degradation process and saturating the reaction[53]. At the same time, a higher number of intermediates could potentially adsorb to the catalyst surface, reducing the degradation rate. The straight line obtained from the linear form of the Langmuir-Hinshelwood model is shown in Fig. 9d. By determining the slope and intercept of the line, the values of the rate constant and adsorption constant can be derived, respectively. The calculated k was 9.5293 mg/(L·h) and the K was 0.1106 L/mg.

The degradation process was significantly impacted by the pH, and the acidity or alkalinity of the solution was known to affect not only the production of free radicals during the photoreaction process but also the adsorption process of pollutants onto the catalyst surface. To investigate the effect of pH on the degradation process, photocatalytic experiments were conducted after the pH of the solution had been adjusted to 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11, respectively, with all other conditions remaining unchanged. The results of the effect of pH on the photocatalytic degradation of BPA by 5 % OCN-BS are shown in Fig. 9e and Fig. 9f. Under acidic conditions, the degradation of BPA by the catalyst was enhanced, with a faster degradation rate and increased degradation efficiency, while under alkaline conditions, the degradation of BPA by the catalyst was weakened. This is because the pH affects the charge state on the surface of the catalyst[10]. The acid dissociation constant (pKa) of BPA is about 10.3, and the results of the zeta potential test of 5 % OCN-BS are shown in Fig. S11. The zero-point charge (pHzpc) of 5 % OCN-BS is 6.60. Therefore, the catalyst will be positively charged when the pH value is lower than 6.60, and it will be negatively charged when the pH value is higher than 6.60.

In order to highlight the role of the heterojunction structure in the structural stability of the catalysts, cyclic experiments were performed to evaluate the stability of the materials. To assess the stability of the 5 % OCN-BS heterojunction, a photodegradation cycling experiment was carried out by adding 30 mg of the catalyst and a solution of 15 mg/L BPA into a quartz tube reactor. The results are shown in Fig. S10a. From the experimental data, it can be clearly observed that the degradation rate of 15 mg/L BPA by 5 % OCN-BS heterojunction only decreased by about 8 % or so after five recycling experiments. During these five cycling experiments, the degradation rate has been stabilized at more than 85 % with almost no significant performance degradation. Comparison with the performance of the FGBSP catalysts shows clear superiority. FGBSP was a photocatalytic material obtained by our direct doping of P into the synthesized CN-BS. As in Fig. S10b, after three cycles of the FGBSP catalyst, the degradation rate decreased by about 30 %, and ultimately could only be maintained at about 60 %. This indicates that the 5 % OCN-BS heterojunction possesses superior stability relative to FGBSP.

In addition, FT-IR tests and XRD tests were performed on the 5 % OCN-BS heterojunction material after undergoing five cycles. The FT-IR test results of the 5 % OCN-BS heterojunction material are shown in Fig. S10c, which shows that there is not much change in the material properties after five cycles. During the photocatalytic process, reactions such as substance adsorption and intermediate product generation occurred on the catalyst surface, potentially leading to changes in the surface functional groups. Consequently, the FT-IR results, which showed no significant changes, indicated that the surface functional groups of the 5 % OCN-BS heterojunction remained stable during the catalytic reaction. It was observed that its structure was not subject to significant depletion or mutation during repeated cycling, suggesting that it possessed the structural stability required for recycling. The XRD patterns before and after 5 % OCN-BS cycling as shown in Fig. S10d were equally unchanged. In photocatalytic reactions, redox reactions may occur on the catalyst surface, and these processes may lead to changes in the crystal structure. However, the results of XRD tests before and after cycling of the 5 % OCN-BS heterojunction illustrated that the heterojunction was able to maintain high stability in catalytic applications. The FT-IR (Fig. S10c) and XDR (Fig. S10d) results indicate that the OCN-BS catalyst exhibits high stability during the catalytic process. The primary cause is attributed to the transfer of electrons and holes between the BS and OCN. The transfer of electrons from the BS to the OCN was responsible for slowing down the rate of photocorrosion in the BS, and also made it difficult for electron-hole pairs on the OCN to rapidly recombine, thereby allowing for the production of a large number of reactive species

To verify the above speculations, ICP was used to measure the dissolution of the metal Bi. The proportion of bismuth metal dissolved in the 5 % OCN-BS heterojunction was found to be only 1.05 %, which was significantly lower than that of the FGBSP catalyst. This result was attributed to the role played by the construction of the 5 % OCN-BS heterojunction. As depicted in Fig. 8, due to the energy level differences between the different materials, electrons were excited and transported directionally from the BS to the CN under illumination, without being trapped on the bismuth sulfide surface. The heterojunction effectively reduced the electron density on the BS surface and decreased the chance of reaction with oxygen, which in turn reduced the probability of generating ·O2 - on the BS surface. This reduction in the generation of ·O2 - decreased the risk of corrosion of BS and improved the stability of the material.

To verify whether BS corrosion was attenuated, XPS characterization was conducted on the surface chemical state of the catalyst before and after the reaction. If photo-corrosion occurred during the photocatalytic process, this could result in a change in the valence state of the metal Bi. By comparing the XPS spectra before and after the photocatalytic reaction, it was possible to observe whether oxidation of the metal Bi had taken place, and thus determine whether photo-corrosion had occurred. Fig. S10e and Fig. S10f displayed the XPS spectra of FGBSP and OCN-BS before and after the reaction, respectively. From these spectra, it was observed that two spin-orbit peaks appeared at 158.2 eV and 163.5 eV for FGBSP, and at 158.1 eV and 163.7 eV for OCN-BS, both corresponding to Bi 4 f7/2 and Bi 4 f5/2 of Bi3+, respectively. In contrast, two additional characteristic peaks were noted at higher binding energies, which overlapped with the main Bi 4 f peak transition and could be attributed to a slight surface charge effect resulting from the change in crystal polarization [54]. However, after the reaction, two new characteristic peaks at 157.7 eV and 163.2 eV, corresponding to Bi-O bonds, were observed in the FGBSP spectrum, whereas no such peaks were detected in the OCN-BS spectrum. This observation suggested that more severe photo-corrosion had occurred in the FGBSP before and after the reaction, whereas the photo-corrosion of OCN-BS was found to be weaker.

Bismuth sulfide-carbon nitride heterojunction photocatalysts (xCN-BS) doped with nonmetallic elements were prepared using a hydrothermal method. The results of photocatalytic experiments indicated that 5 % OCN-BS degraded 15 mg/L BPA by 96 % within 4 h, demonstrating the excellent photocatalytic performance of xCN-BS. The energy band structure of xCN-BS was analyzed, revealing that the introduction of nonmetallic elements narrowed the bandgap and optimized the electronic energy band structure of xCN-BS. The xCN-BS heterojunction materials were optimized in the photocatalytic reaction due to the intrinsic differences between the xCN and BS materials. These differences generate a built-in electric field, which enables the efficient transport of excited electrons from the BS to the CN surface. This process slows down the occurrence of photocorrosion on the BS surface. The built-in electric field enhances the photocatalytic performance of xCN-BS in degrading pollutants, while the presence of xCN prevents the dissolution of metallic Bi in BS, thereby further improving the stability of the material. This dual effect achieves the goal of “killing two birds with one stone.” This study primarily emphasizes the benefits of the built-in electric field to the photocatalytic reaction system. Future research can focus on preparing new heterojunction photocatalytic materials from the perspective of constructing built-in electric fields, providing new insights for the development of photocatalytic degradation materials.
